nodes.title: Web Hacking: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Web Hacking. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A login form concatenates user input directly into the SQL statement without parameterization. The attacker enters the username `admin' --` and any password, and is logged in as admin. Which web-attack class is this and what is the precise mechanism?
flashcards.back: Concatenating untrusted input into SQL is the textbook SQL-injection class. The single quote closes the username literal and the `--` comments out everything after it on that line — so the WHERE clause becomes `WHERE username='admin'`, the password test is dropped, and the application authenticates the attacker as admin. This is an in-band (classic / tautology) SQLi used for authentication bypass. Parameterized queries / prepared statements remove the attack surface entirely. 'Reflected XSS' injects script into a rendered response, not into a SQL statement. 'CSRF' rides an already-authenticated session — it does not bypass authentication. 'LDAP injection' uses LDAP filter metacharacters (`*`, `(`, `)`, `&`, `|`) against a directory server, not SQL.

flashcards.front: A single-page application reads its hash fragment via `location.hash` and writes it straight into `innerHTML`. An attacker shares a link of the form `https://app.example/#`. The payload never reaches the server. Which XSS variant is this?
flashcards.back: DOM-based XSS occurs entirely client-side: a script reads attacker-controlled data from a DOM source (here `location.hash`) and passes it to a dangerous DOM sink (here `innerHTML`) without the server ever seeing the payload — browser fragments are not sent in HTTP requests. The fix is to use safe sinks (`textContent`, framework-bound templates) or contextual escaping such as DOMPurify. 'Reflected XSS' would require the server to echo the payload back in its response, which does not happen with a fragment. 'Stored XSS' would require persistence on the server. 'Blind XSS' describes WHERE the payload eventually fires (in an admin console invisible to the attacker), not how it is delivered — and the question is about delivery mechanics.

flashcards.front: A web app sets its session cookie without the HttpOnly and Secure flags, and reflects unsanitized input into the page. An attacker wants to steal live sessions at scale. Which chained attack is MOST effective and which single cookie flag would blunt the theft step?
flashcards.back: Unsanitized reflected input plus a script-readable cookie is the classic XSS-to-session-hijack chain: injected JavaScript reads `document.cookie` and sends it to an attacker endpoint. Setting HttpOnly removes the cookie from the DOM/JavaScript scope, so even a successful XSS payload cannot read it. The Secure flag only forces HTTPS transport (it does not stop a script read), SameSite mitigates cross-site request forgery rather than script-based theft, and SQL injection against a session table is not what the reflected-input weakness enables here.

flashcards.front: A tester finds a parameter that fetches a URL supplied by the client so the server can pull a preview image. They make the server request `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`. Which vulnerability class is this, and what is the primary risk on a cloud host?
flashcards.back: When a server fetches an attacker-controlled URL, the attacker can pivot the server's trust to reach internal endpoints — the hallmark of SSRF. On many cloud instances the link-local metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) returns instance role credentials, so an unguarded fetch can leak temporary keys and escalate into the cloud account (the reason IMDSv2 and egress controls exist). CSRF abuses a victim's browser, LFI reads local files via path traversal, and an open redirect merely bounces a user — none of which describe the server itself making an internal request.

questions.q: A login form concatenates user input directly into the SQL statement without parameterization. The attacker enters the username `admin' --` and any password, and is logged in as admin. Which web-attack class is this and what is the precise mechanism?
choices: Reflected cross-site scripting — the attacker's payload is echoed back into the response and executes in the victim's browser
In-band SQL injection (authentication bypass via comment) — the `--` comments out the rest of the WHERE clause, including the password check
Cross-site request forgery — the victim's authenticated browser is tricked into submitting a state-changing request to the application
LDAP injection — operators such as `*)(&` are injected into a directory-search filter to broaden the result set
questions.explanation: Concatenating untrusted input into SQL is the textbook SQL-injection class. The single quote closes the username literal and the `--` comments out everything after it on that line — so the WHERE clause becomes `WHERE username='admin'`, the password test is dropped, and the application authenticates the attacker as admin. This is an in-band (classic / tautology) SQLi used for authentication bypass. Parameterized queries / prepared statements remove the attack surface entirely. 'Reflected XSS' injects script into a rendered response, not into a SQL statement. 'CSRF' rides an already-authenticated session — it does not bypass authentication. 'LDAP injection' uses LDAP filter metacharacters (`*`, `(`, `)`, `&`, `|`) against a directory server, not SQL.

questions.q: A single-page application reads its hash fragment via `location.hash` and writes it straight into `innerHTML`. An attacker shares a link of the form `https://app.example/#`. The payload never reaches the server. Which XSS variant is this?
choices: Reflected (Type-I) XSS — the payload travels through the server in a query parameter and is reflected back into the rendered HTML response
Stored (Type-II) XSS — the payload is persisted in a database or filesystem and served back to any later visitor
DOM-based (Type-0) XSS — the malicious data flows from a client-side source into a client-side sink without ever leaving the browser
Blind XSS — the payload fires only inside an administrative interface that the attacker themselves cannot directly observe
questions.explanation: DOM-based XSS occurs entirely client-side: a script reads attacker-controlled data from a DOM source (here `location.hash`) and passes it to a dangerous DOM sink (here `innerHTML`) without the server ever seeing the payload — browser fragments are not sent in HTTP requests. The fix is to use safe sinks (`textContent`, framework-bound templates) or contextual escaping such as DOMPurify. 'Reflected XSS' would require the server to echo the payload back in its response, which does not happen with a fragment. 'Stored XSS' would require persistence on the server. 'Blind XSS' describes WHERE the payload eventually fires (in an admin console invisible to the attacker), not how it is delivered — and the question is about delivery mechanics.

questions.q: A web app sets its session cookie without the HttpOnly and Secure flags, and reflects unsanitized input into the page. An attacker wants to steal live sessions at scale. Which chained attack is MOST effective and which single cookie flag would blunt the theft step?
choices: CSRF to change the victim's password; the SameSite flag stops it.
SQL injection to dump the session table; the Secure flag stops it.
Reflected/stored XSS that reads document.cookie and exfiltrates it; the HttpOnly flag stops the cookie read.
Clickjacking via an invisible iframe; the HttpOnly flag stops it.
questions.explanation: Unsanitized reflected input plus a script-readable cookie is the classic XSS-to-session-hijack chain: injected JavaScript reads `document.cookie` and sends it to an attacker endpoint. Setting HttpOnly removes the cookie from the DOM/JavaScript scope, so even a successful XSS payload cannot read it. The Secure flag only forces HTTPS transport (it does not stop a script read), SameSite mitigates cross-site request forgery rather than script-based theft, and SQL injection against a session table is not what the reflected-input weakness enables here.

questions.q: A tester finds a parameter that fetches a URL supplied by the client so the server can pull a preview image. They make the server request `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`. Which vulnerability class is this, and what is the primary risk on a cloud host?
choices: Local File Inclusion (LFI); it reads /etc/passwd from the web root.
Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF); it forces the victim's browser to submit a form.
Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF); it can reach the instance metadata service and expose temporary cloud credentials.
Open redirect; it only sends the user to an attacker page.
questions.explanation: When a server fetches an attacker-controlled URL, the attacker can pivot the server's trust to reach internal endpoints — the hallmark of SSRF. On many cloud instances the link-local metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) returns instance role credentials, so an unguarded fetch can leak temporary keys and escalate into the cloud account (the reason IMDSv2 and egress controls exist). nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: An attacker who has extracted NTLM hashes from a compromised Windows host re-authenticates to other servers using the raw hash, without ever cracking it to plaintext. Which underlying weakness makes a Pass-the-Hash attack possible?
choices: Local Security Authority Subsystem Service caches the user's plaintext password indefinitely in process memory
NTLM authentication treats the password hash itself as the credential — the protocol never requires the plaintext to be presented
The SAM database stores account passwords using a reversible encryption that the attacker can decrypt with the boot key
Kerberos pre-authentication is downgraded to RC4-HMAC whenever a workstation joins a legacy domain
questions.explanation: In NTLM, the client proves knowledge of the password by encrypting a server-supplied challenge with a key derived from the password hash. The hash is therefore functionally equivalent to the password — anyone holding it can complete the challenge/response, so cracking it to plaintext is unnecessary. Mitigations are LAPS, restricted-admin / credential guard, tiered admin and disabling NTLM where possible. 'LSASS caches plaintext' is wrong on modern Windows: it caches credential material in a form usable for SSO, but Credential Guard isolates this and patched Windows does not retain reusable plaintext for interactive logons by default. 'SAM stores reversible encryption' is false — SAM stores LM/NTLM hashes (one-way), not reversible ciphertext. 'Kerberos downgrade to RC4' enables Kerberoasting/AS-REP attacks, which are distinct from PtH and do not rely on NTLM at all.

questions.q: A red team has a low-privilege shell on a Windows host and recovers the local SAM. Rather than cracking the NTLM hashes offline, the operator wants to authenticate to other hosts that share the local admin password. Which technique fits, and what control most directly defeats it?
choices: Pass-the-Hash using the NTLM hash directly against SMB; defeated by enforcing unique local admin passwords via LAPS and enabling SMB signing.
Kerberoasting the service accounts; defeated by rotating the KRBTGT key twice.
Golden Ticket forgery; defeated by shortening the maximum ticket lifetime.
LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning; defeated by deploying a WSUS server.
questions.explanation: NTLM authentication proves knowledge of the hash, not the plaintext, so a captured hash can be replayed directly (Pass-the-Hash) without cracking. When every workstation shares the same local Administrator password, one hash unlocks the fleet — Microsoft LAPS randomizes each machine's local admin password to break that lateral path, and SMB signing hardens the session. Kerberoasting targets service-account TGS tickets (a different attack against domain SPNs). A Golden Ticket requires the KRBTGT hash, which a local SAM does not contain. LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning is a name-resolution capture technique, unrelated to replaying a recovered SAM hash.

questions.q: An attacker is plugged into a modern switched LAN and wants to capture traffic flowing between two other hosts on the same VLAN that they are not on the path of. Which technique enables this on commodity switches without special hardware?
choices: Enabling promiscuous mode on the attacker's NIC so it accepts frames addressed to other MACs
Performing a DNS zone transfer (AXFR) against the segment's primary nameserver
Requesting that the switch mirror the relevant ports to the attacker via SPAN / port-mirroring
Poisoning the ARP caches of the two victims so each one resolves the other's IP to the attacker's MAC
questions.explanation: ARP spoofing inserts the attacker as a transparent man-in-the-middle: by sending unsolicited ARP replies, each victim caches the attacker's MAC for the other's IP, so the switch then forwards their frames to the attacker, who relays them after sniffing. Defences are Dynamic ARP Inspection, DHCP snooping bindings, and static ARP for critical hosts. 'Promiscuous mode' is necessary to read frames the NIC receives but a switch will not deliver other hosts' unicast frames to that port in the first place. 'DNS zone transfer' enumerates DNS records — useful for footprinting, but not a sniffing primitive on the LAN. 'SPAN / port-mirroring' would work, but it requires administrative access to the switch (the attacker normally does not have it) — the question asks how to do this on commodity switches without that level of access.

questions.q: An attacker on the same subnet as a target sends a stream of gratuitous ARP replies mapping the default gateway's IP to the attacker's MAC. What is the immediate effect, and which control most directly prevents it on a managed switch?
choices: It exhausts the DHCP pool (starvation); prevented by port security limiting MAC counts.
It poisons victims' ARP caches so their gateway-bound traffic flows through the attacker (MITM); prevented by Dynamic ARP Inspection tied to DHCP snooping.
It floods the CAM table so the switch fails open; prevented by BPDU guard.
It performs a SYN flood against the gateway; prevented by SYN cookies.
questions.explanation: Unsolicited (gratuitous) ARP replies overwrite the victims' cached IP-to-MAC mapping for the gateway, so their outbound traffic is sent to the attacker — a classic ARP-poisoning man-in-the-middle. Dynamic ARP Inspection validates ARP packets against the DHCP snooping binding table and drops forged mappings, which directly stops it. DHCP starvation, CAM-table flooding, and SYN floods are separate attacks; port security, BPDU guard, and SYN cookies address those other cases, not ARP cache poisoning.

questions.q: WPA2-Personal is vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks against captured four-way handshakes (and the PMKID variant against single beacons). Which specific WPA3-Personal mechanism makes that offline cracking infeasible?
choices: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE / Dragonfly) — a password-authenticated key exchange that requires an online guess per attempt and provides forward secrecy
Mandatory 192-bit Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite — required for every WPA3-Personal client and AP regardless of deployment
Static rotation of the GTK (Group Temporal Key) every 60 seconds, derived from the pre-shared key with no client interaction
Caching of the PMKID inside Beacon and Probe-Response frames so roaming clients can re-associate without re-authenticating
questions.explanation: SAE (a.k.a. Dragonfly) is a password-authenticated key exchange: each guess at the password requires a full online handshake with the AP, so capturing frames and cracking offline at GPU speeds — the entire WPA2 PSK attack model — stops working. SAE also provides forward secrecy, so even a future password disclosure does not decrypt previously captured sessions. The 192-bit CNSA suite is associated with WPA3-Enterprise, not Personal — calling it 'mandatory for every WPA3 client' is wrong. Periodic GTK rotation existed in WPA2 and is unrelated to PSK offline cracking. PMKID caching in Beacons/Probe-Responses is precisely the WPA2 weakness Jens Steube exploited; WPA3 does not advertise PMKID this way.

questions.q: A tester captures the WPA2-PSK 4-way handshake for a target SSID and wants to recover the passphrase offline. Which statement about the attack is accurate?
choices: The handshake lets you decrypt all past traffic immediately without knowing the passphrase, because the PMK is transmitted in frame 2.
The attack only works if WPS is enabled, because the PSK is derived from the WPS PIN.
Capturing the handshake is unnecessary; WPA2-PSK keys can always be read from the beacon frames.
You must perform an offline dictionary/brute-force attack: the handshake enables verifying candidate passphrases against the captured MIC, so a strong passphrase defeats it.
questions.explanation: The WPA2-PSK 4-way handshake never transmits the PSK or PMK; it exchanges nonces and a MIC. Capturing it lets an attacker test candidate passphrases offline — derive the PMK from a guess plus the SSID, compute the PTK and MIC, and compare to the captured MIC. This makes passphrase strength the whole defense: a long, random passphrase is computationally infeasible to brute-force. The PMK is not sent in frame 2, keys are not present in beacons, and while a separate WPS PIN attack exists, WPA2-PSK cracking via handshake capture does not depend on WPS.

questions.q: A pentester recovers a database of unsalted MD5 password hashes and cracks 70% of them in minutes using a precomputed rainbow table. Which defensive change at the application layer would have made this specific attack effectively useless?
choices: Switching the storage algorithm from MD5 to SHA-1 while keeping the hashes unsalted
Generating a unique random salt per password and storing it alongside the hash, ideally combined with a memory-hard KDF such as bcrypt / Argon2
Wrapping each stored hash with AES-128 encryption using a key kept inside the same database server
Truncating the resulting hash to 64 bits so that fewer characters need to be presented at login time
questions.explanation: A unique random salt per password makes every hash unique even when users pick the same password, which renders precomputed tables (rainbow tables, lookup tables) useless — an attacker would need to build one table per salt, defeating the precomputation. Pairing the salt with a memory-hard KDF (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2id) additionally slows each guess by orders of magnitude. 'SHA-1 unsalted' just swaps one fast unsalted hash for another and is itself broken — rainbow tables exist for SHA-1 as well. 'AES-wrap with a key on the same server' fails the assumed threat model: if the attacker dumped the hashes, they almost certainly also have the key. 'Truncate to 64 bits' makes brute force EASIER (smaller search space) and increases collisions; it is the opposite of what is needed.

questions.q: An organization asks whether MD5 is acceptable for storing user passwords. As the ethical hacker, which recommendation is correct and why?
choices: MD5 is fine if each password is salted, because salting makes MD5 collision-resistant.
Encrypt passwords with AES-256 so they can be decrypted and re-hashed later.
Switch to SHA-256 without a salt, since a longer digest alone stops rainbow tables.
MD5 is unacceptable for passwords; use a slow, salted, purpose-built KDF such as bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 to resist GPU brute-forcing.
questions.explanation: MD5 is extremely fast and thus ideal for attackers — modern GPUs test billions of MD5 guesses per second — and salting only defeats precomputed rainbow tables, not fast brute-forcing. Password storage should use a deliberately slow, memory-hard KDF (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2) with a per-user salt and a tunable work factor. Plain SHA-256 is still fast even with a salt, and reversibly encrypting passwords with AES is an anti-pattern because a key compromise exposes every plaintext at once.
